claim: Vimentin is a type III intermediate filament (IF) protein that is induced in a large number of solid tumours.
source: Vimentin is a type III intermediate filament (IF) protein that is induced in a large number of solid tumours.
evidence: This is a general statement about vimentin's classification and expression pattern in tumors, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: A single cysteine at position 328 in vimentin plays a crucial role in assembly, organisation, and stability of IFs.
source: A single cysteine at position 328 in vimentin plays a crucial role in assembly, organisation, and stability of IFs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the manuscript.

claim: The expression of C328-VIM impacted vimentin–actin interactions and induced EMT-like features that include enhanced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion accompanied by reduced cell adhesion when compared to the wildtype cells.
source: The expression of C328-VIM impacted vimentin–actin interactions and induced EMT-like features that include enhanced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion accompanied by reduced cell adhesion when compared to the wildtype cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including functional assays and microscopy.

claim: Functional transcriptomic studies confirmed the upregulation of EMT and mesenchymal markers, downregulation of epithelial markers, as well as acquisition of signatures associated with cancer stemness (CD56, POU5F1, PROCR, and CD49f).
source: Functional transcriptomic studies confirmed the upregulation of EMT and mesenchymal markers, downregulation of epithelial markers, as well as acquisition of signatures associated with cancer stemness (CD56, POU5F1, PROCR, and CD49f), thus transforming MCF-7 cells from oestrogen-positive to triple-reduced (ESR1, PGR, and HER2) status.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and validation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: C328-VIM expression transformed MCF-7 cells from oestrogen-positive to triple-reduced (ESR1, PGR, and HER2) status.
source: Functional transcriptomic studies confirmed the upregulation of EMT and mesenchymal markers, downregulation of epithelial markers, as well as acquisition of signatures associated with cancer stemness (CD56, POU5F1, PROCR, and CD49f), thus transforming MCF-7 cells from oestrogen-positive to triple-reduced (ESR1, PGR, and HER2) status.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data showing downregulation of ESR1, PGR, and HER2.

claim: There was a stark increase in the expression of long non-coding RNA, XIST, in MCF-7 cells expressing C328-VIM.
source: We also observed a stark increase in the expression of long non-coding RNA, XIST, in MCF-7 cells expressing C328-VIM.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data showing XIST as the most upregulated gene.

claim: Targeting the mutant vimentin or XIST by RNA interference partially reversed the phenotypes in C328-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells.
source: Targeting the mutant vimentin or XIST by RNA interference partially reversed the phenotypes in C328-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from shRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: The introduction of C328-VIM cells into nude mice promoted tumour growth by increasing cancer stemness in an oestrogen-independent manner.
source: Furthermore, the introduction of C328-VIM cells into nude mice promoted tumour growth by increasing cancer stemness in an oestrogen-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo transplantation experiments and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Vimentin is one of the most extensively studied IFs due to its diverse pathophysiological role(s).
source: Due to its diverse pathophysiological role(s), it is one of the most extensively studied IFs.
evidence: This is a general statement about the research focus on vimentin, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Vimentin has been proposed to play a role in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and cancer metastasis.
source: It has been proposed to play a role in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and cancer metastasis (Usman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vimentin plays a role in normal positioning of cell organelles, nuclear and DNA integrity.
source: It is a structurally dynamic protein active in cell mechanics (Patteson et al., 2020), normal positioning of cell organelles, nuclear and DNA integrity (Danielsson et al., 2018), stress response (Mónico et al., 2019), autophagy (Surolia and Antony, 2022), cell proliferation, migration (Wang et al., 2019), adhesion, invasion (Wang et al., 2021), signalling, angiogenesis (Chen et al., 2021), and immune responses (Ridge et al., 2022).

claim: The complete crystal structure of vimentin is still not available.
source: The complete crystal structure of vimentin is still not available; however, crystal structures of small segments have been investigated (Strelkov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of structural knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Crystal structures of small segments of vimentin have been investigated.
source: The complete crystal structure of vimentin is still not available; however, crystal structures of small segments have been investigated (Strelkov et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Strelkov et al., 2002.

claim: Vimentin monomer has a central α-helical rod domain flanked by non-helical head and tail domains on each side.
source: Structurally, vimentin monomer has a central α-helical rod domain flanked by non-helical head and tail domains on each side (Chernyatina et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chernyatina et al., 2012.

claim: Vimentin monomers assemble in parallel to form dimers, with two dimers assembling in antiparallel to form tetramers.
source: Studies have described its polymerisation in which monomers assemble in parallel to form dimers, with two dimers assembling in antiparallel to form tetramers (Herrmann and Aebi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herrmann and Aebi, 2016.

claim: Eight tetramers combine to form unit length filaments (ULFs) that further assemble head to tail into 10 nm compact mature filaments.
source: Eight tetramers combine to form unit length filaments (ULFs) that further assemble head to tail into 10 nm compact mature filaments (Nunes Vicente et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nunes Vicente et al., 2022.

claim: IFs lack polarity and in mature filaments subunits continue to assemble at both ends.
source: IFs lack polarity and in mature filaments subunits continue to assemble at both ends, and they can be exchanged anywhere along the whole filament length, a process that requires ATP (Robert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robert et al., 2015.

claim: Subunits in mature vimentin filaments can be exchanged anywhere along the whole filament length, a process that requires ATP.
source: IFs lack polarity and in mature filaments subunits continue to assemble at both ends, and they can be exchanged anywhere along the whole filament length, a process that requires ATP (Robert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robert et al., 2015.

claim: Vimentin directly interacts with actin through its tail domain to maintain mechanical integrity of the cell and cytoskeletal crosstalk.
source: Vimentin directly interacts with actin through its tail domain to maintain mechanical integrity of the cell and cytoskeletal crosstalk (Esue et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Esue et al., 2006.

claim: Vimentin C328 is reported to be a stress sensor induced by oxidants and electrophiles, resulting in its zinc-mediated modifications and consequently disassembly or rearrangement of filaments as a stress response.
source: Vimentin has a single cysteine residue at position 328 in the rod domain, which is reported to be a stress sensor induced by oxidants and electrophiles, resulting in its zinc-mediated modifications and consequently disassembly or rearrangement of filaments as a stress response (Mónico et al., 2019; Pérez-Sala et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mónico et al., 2019 and Pérez-Sala et al., 2015.

claim: Different modifications of C328 have been reported during cellular senescence, rheumatoid arthritis, cataract, and atherosclerosis.
source: Different modifications of C328 that have been reported during cellular senescence, rheumatoid arthritis, cataract, and atherosclerosis (Viedma-Poyatos et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Viedma-Poyatos et al., 2020.

claim: Any mutation or modification in C328 can hamper the intracellular stress response of vimentin.
source: Any mutation or modification in C328 can hamper the intracellular stress response of vimentin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of C328 in stress response.

claim: C328 residue has been reported to have widespread pathophysiological implications and is considered a flash point for stress ignition.
source: Therefore, this residue has been reported to have widespread pathophysiological implications and is considered a flash point for stress ignition (Viedma-Poyatos et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Viedma-Poyatos et al., 2020.

claim: The role of vimentin C328 in regulating EMT, tumour growth, and progression has not been studied.
source: Although the role of vimenetin C328 in response to cellular stress has been studied in some detail, its role in regulating EMT, tumour growth, and progression has not been studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing research.

claim: MCF-7 is a vimentin-deficient cell line.
source: To investigate the functional implications of vimentin residue C328 in regulating EMT, cancer progression, and stemness, we expressed C328S vimentin in MCF-7 cells, a vimentin-deficient cell line (Usman et al., 2022a) commonly employed to study EMT (Guttilla et al., 2012; Kondaveeti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MCF-7 is commonly employed to study EMT.
source: To investigate the functional implications of vimentin residue C328 in regulating EMT, cancer progression, and stemness, we expressed C328S vimentin in MCF-7 cells, a vimentin-deficient cell line (Usman et al., 2022a) commonly employed to study EMT (Guttilla et al., 2012; Kondaveeti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guttilla et al., 2012 and Kondaveeti et al., 2015.

claim: C328S-VIM altered cell morphology with disorganised F-actin and induced EMT and cancer stem cell characteristics.
source: Our findings reveal that C328S-VIM altered cell morphology with disorganised F-actin and induced EMT and cancer stem cell characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: XIST is a long non-coding RNA that was upregulated in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells.
source: A highly significant observation was the upregulation of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), XIST, in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells, which are normally oestrogen-dependent for tumorigenesis (Soule and McGrath, 1980), becoming oestrogen-independent by C328S-VIM in nude mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MCF-7 cells are normally oestrogen-dependent for tumorigenesis.
source: A highly significant observation was the upregulation of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), XIST, in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells, which are normally oestrogen-dependent for tumorigenesis (Soule and McGrath, 1980), becoming oestrogen-independent by C328S-VIM in nude mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Soule and McGrath, 1980.

claim: MCF-7 cells expressing C328S-VIM became oestrogen-independent in nude mice.
source: A highly significant observation was the upregulation of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), XIST, in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells, which are normally oestrogen-dependent for tumorigenesis (Soule and McGrath, 1980), becoming oestrogen-independent by C328S-VIM in nude mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo transplantation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: C328S-VIM can trigger an EMT programme and enhance stemness in MCF-7 cells, in part via XIST upregulation.
source: We show that C328S-VIM can trigger an EMT programme and enhance stemness in MCF-7 cells, in part via XIST upregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including RNA-Seq and knockdown experiments.

claim: Numerous vimentin variants have been reported in the vicinity of the C328 residue in several solid tumours.
source: These findings have far-reaching implications, particularly considering the numerous vimentin variants reported in the vicinity of the C328 residue in several solid tumours (Usman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Usman et al., 2021.

claim: The wildtype and mutant vimentin proteins were equally expressed in MCF-7 cells.
source: The quantification of the relevant bands showed that the wildtype and mutant vimentin proteins were equally expressed in MCF-7 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Wildtype vimentin showed a fully extended vimentin network from perinuclear to peripheral cell boundaries in MCF-7 cells.
source: Immunostaining of the wildtype vimentin showed a fully extended vimentin network from perinuclear to peripheral cell boundaries, whereas in cells transduced with the C328S mutant, the vimentin was more condensed around the perinuclear area (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In cells transduced with the C328S mutant, the vimentin was more condensed around the perinuclear area.
source: Immunostaining of the wildtype vimentin showed a fully extended vimentin network from perinuclear to peripheral cell boundaries, whereas in cells transduced with the C328S mutant, the vimentin was more condensed around the perinuclear area (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: C328S-VIM retains its ability to polymerise into filaments both in A431 and MCF-7 cells.
source: This shows that C328S-VIM retains its ability to polymerise into filaments both in A431 and MCF-7 cells; however, in MCF-7 these filaments were drastically reorganised, affecting the cell shape (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1D.

claim: In MCF-7 cells, C328S-VIM filaments were drastically reorganised, affecting the cell shape.
source: This shows that C328S-VIM retains its ability to polymerise into filaments both in A431 and MCF-7 cells; however, in MCF-7 these filaments were drastically reorganised, affecting the cell shape (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both untagged and AcGFP-C328S-VIM constructs were not dominant negative as they did not disturb the pre-existing filaments and appeared to integrate into the pre-existing network.
source: Our data showed that both untagged and AcGFP-C328S-VIM constructs were not dominant negative as they did not disturb the pre-existing filaments and appeared to integrate into the pre-existing network.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: The thiol group of C328 enables specific hydrogen bonding and potential disulphide-mediated interactions with actin.
source: It should be noted that the thiol group of C328 enables specific hydrogen bonding and potential disulphide-mediated interactions with actin (González-Jiménez et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to González-Jiménez et al., 2023.

claim: The C328S mutation induced alterations within the coiled-coil rod domain of vimentin, particularly in regions critical for actin binding.
source: The computational results revealed that the C328S mutation induced alterations within the coiled-coil rod domain of vimentin, particularly in regions critical for actin binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The substitution of cysteine with serine likely altered the conformation of hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts, thus weakening the overall binding affinity of the mutant vimentin for actin.
source: The substitution of cysteine with serine likely altered the conformation of hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts, thus weakening the overall binding affinity of the mutant vimentin for actin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on in silico modeling results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: C328S-VIM-expressing cells showed low-level F-actin/stress fibre staining with aggregates/fragments at the cortical margins of the cells with no stress fibres in the centres of the cells compared with high-level F-actin/stress fibre staining in WT.
source: Quantification of stress fibre/F-actin staining pattern as described previously (Avraham-Chakim et al., 2013) confirmed that actin morphology and organisation was altered with low-level F-actin/stress fibre staining with aggregates/fragments at the cortical margins of the cells. No stress fibres were observed in the centres of the cells in C328S-VIM-expressing cells compared with high-level F-actin/stress fibre staining in WT (Figure 1F and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; compare A with B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining and quantification data shown in Figure 1F, 1G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: C328S-VIM when expressed in MCF-7 cells alters cell morphology through remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: These data show that C328S-VIM when expressed in MCF-7 cells alters cell morphology through remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on F-actin staining and cell morphology analysis.

claim: C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells showed more cellular projections when compared to WT.
source: C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells showed more cellular projections when compared to WT and analysis of nuclear area, nuclear form factor, nuclear major axis, nuclear minor axis, cell area, cell diameter, cell perimeter, cell minor axis, cell major axis, and cell form factor were significantly (p<0.05) increased (Figure 2C), while the nucleus/cell area ratio and cell compactness were significantly decreased in cells expressing C328S-VIM in comparison to WT-VIM-expressing cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Nuclear area, nuclear form factor, nuclear major axis, nuclear minor axis, cell area, cell diameter, cell perimeter, cell minor axis, cell major axis, and cell form factor were significantly increased in C328S-VIM-expressing cells.
source: C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells showed more cellular projections when compared to WT and analysis of nuclear area, nuclear form factor, nuclear major axis, nuclear minor axis, cell area, cell diameter, cell perimeter, cell minor axis, cell major axis, and cell form factor were significantly (p<0.05) increased (Figure 2C), while the nucleus/cell area ratio and cell compactness were significantly decreased in cells expressing C328S-VIM in comparison to WT-VIM-expressing cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The nucleus/cell area ratio and cell compactness were significantly decreased in cells expressing C328S-VIM in comparison to WT-VIM-expressing cells.
source: C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells showed more cellular projections when compared to WT and analysis of nuclear area, nuclear form factor, nuclear major axis, nuclear minor axis, cell area, cell diameter, cell perimeter, cell minor axis, cell major axis, and cell form factor were significantly (p<0.05) increased (Figure 2C), while the nucleus/cell area ratio and cell compactness were significantly decreased in cells expressing C328S-VIM in comparison to WT-VIM-expressing cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The expression of C328S-VIM significantly altered nuclear and cell perimeter as evident by more ruffled margins in MCF-7 cells.
source: These results indicate that the expression of C328S-VIM significantly altered nuclear and cell perimeter as evident by more ruffled margins in MCF-7 cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis data.

claim: C328S cells showed a highly significant increase in cell proliferation and mitochondrial activity compared to WT cells.
source: The analyses showed a highly significant increase in cell proliferation and mitochondrial activity in C328S compared to WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by colony formation, MTT, and CyQUANT proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells showed reduced adhesion without substrate coating on the culture vessel.
source: Furthermore, C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells showed reduced adhesion without substrate coating on the culture vessel as determined by the CyQUANT cell adhesion assay (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: When the tissue culture plates were coated with different substrates such as laminin, fibronectin, and collagen, there was no significant difference in cell adhesion between WT and C328S cells.
source: However, when the tissue culture plates were coated with different substrates such as laminin, fibronectin, and collagen, there was no significant difference in cell adhesion (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The number of cells migrating through the membrane was significantly higher in C328S compared with the WT cells.
source: The chemotactic migration of the cells towards foetal calf serum (FCS) through 8 µm pore size culture inserts showed the number of cells migrating through the membrane was significantly higher (p<0.05) in C328S compared with the WT cells (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by chemotactic migration assay data shown in Figure 2K and 2L.

claim: A significantly higher number of cells invaded through Matrigel in C328S-VIM compared with the WT-VIM.
source: Similarly, the invasive capacity of the two cell lines was compared by coating the 8 µm pore size culture inserts with Matrigel. The results indicated a significantly higher number of cells invading through Matrigel in C328S-VIM (p<0.05) compared with the WT-VIM (Figure 2M and N).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 2M and 2N.

claim: A total of 3421 out of 22,645 genes were significantly upregulated in C328S-VIM vs WT-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells.
source: The analysis showed that a total of 3421 out of 22,645 genes were significantly upregulated, whereas 3940 genes were downregulated (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 3940 genes were downregulated in C328S-VIM vs WT-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells.
source: The analysis showed that a total of 3421 out of 22,645 genes were significantly upregulated, whereas 3940 genes were downregulated (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The significantly downregulated genes are involved in cell–cell adhesion, DNA packaging complex, and keratinocyte differentiation.
source: Functional Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed that the significantly downregulated genes are involved in cell–cell adhesion, DNA packaging complex, and keratinocyte differentiation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The most upregulated cellular function was pattern-specific processes, regionalisation, and related to development.
source: The most upregulated cellular function was pattern-specific processes, regionalisation, and related to development (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The most upregulated gene was XIST, a long non-coding oncogenic RNA (lncRNA) that is implicated in a large number of tumours.
source: The most upregulated gene was XIST (Figure 3D), a long non-coding oncogenic RNA (lncRNA) that is implicated in a large number of tumours (Figure 3E; Madhi and Kim, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Madhi and Kim, 2019.

claim: The RNA-Seq data showed significant Pearson correlation (R2=0.77, p=0.003, Pearson r=0.88) with RT-qPCR validation.
source: The RNA-Seq data was validated using RT-qPCR, and the regression analysis between two data sets showed significant Pearson correlation (R2=0.77, p=0.003, Pearson r=0.88; Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The widespread downregulation of keratin gene expression shown by RNA-Seq and qPCR was corroborated by immunostaining of K8 and K18 and western blotting.
source: The widespread downregulation of keratin gene expression shown by RNA-Seq and qPCR was corroborated by immunostaining of K8 and K18 (Figure 3G) and western blotting (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: K8, K18, K19 were significantly downregulated and TWIST1 and CDH2/N-cadherin were upregulated in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells compared with the WT-VIM-expressing cells.
source: The quantification of the relative band intensity showed significant downregulation in K8, K18, K19 and upregulation of TWIST1 and CDH2/N-cadherin in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells compared with the WT-VIM-expressing cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Multiple epithelial markers were downregulated, and mesenchymal markers were upregulated among DEGs, indicating acquisition of EMT-like characteristics by C328S cells.
source: The RNA-Seq analysis shows that multiple epithelial markers were downregulated, and mesenchymal markers were upregulated among DEGs, indicating acquisition of EMT-like characteristics by C328S cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 4—source data 1and Figure 3—figure supplement 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The RNA-Seq data showed upregulation of EMT transcription factors, including ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST 1, TWIST 2, ETS1, LEF1, SNAI2, and FOXC2, although SNAI1 was downregulated.
source: The RNA-Seq data showed upregulation of EMT transcription factors, including ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST 1, TWIST 2, ETS1, LEF1, SNAI2, and FOXC2, although SNAI1 was downregulated (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The upregulated differentially expressed breast cancer stem cell markers included CD56/NCAM1, POU5F1, PROCR/CD201, ITGA6.
source: The upregulated differentially expressed breast cancer stem cell markers included CD56/NCAM1, POU5F1, PROCR/CD201, ITGA6, and the downregulated were ESR1, PGR, HER2/ERBB2, ABCG2, CD44, CD24, EPCAM, and CDH1 (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The downregulated breast cancer stem cell markers were ESR1, PGR, HER2/ERBB2, ABCG2, CD44, CD24, EPCAM, and CDH1.
source: The upregulated differentially expressed breast cancer stem cell markers included CD56/NCAM1, POU5F1, PROCR/CD201, ITGA6, and the downregulated were ESR1, PGR, HER2/ERBB2, ABCG2, CD44, CD24, EPCAM, and CDH1 (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: MCF-7, which are triple-positive cells, became triple reduced by the expression of C328S-VIM.
source: Out of the presence or absence of three of them, ESR1 (oestrogen receptor), PGR (progesterone receptor), and HER2/ERBB2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2/HER2) make a breast cancer triple positive or triple negative. Our results show that MCF-7, which are triple-positive cells (Comşa et al., 2015), became triple reduced by the expression of C328S-VIM.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data showing downregulation of ESR1, PGR, and HER2/ERBB2, and a citation to Comşa et al., 2015.

claim: C328S-VIM in MCF-7 induces EMT-like characteristics and increases cancer stemness.
source: Collectively these results imply that C328S-VIM in MCF-7 induces EMT-like characteristics and increases cancer stemness.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the RNA-Seq and functional assay data.

claim: MFI of CD56 and CD201 in C328S-VIM cells was significantly higher (p<0.0001) compared with WT-VIM cells.
source: Data analysis using FlowJo v10 confirmed significant upregulation of breast cancer stem cell markers CD56/NCAM1 and CD201/PROCR in C328S-VIM-expressing MCF-7 cells. MFI of CD56 and CD201 in C328S-VIM cells was significantly higher (p<0.0001) compared with WT-VIM cells (Figure 3L–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: C328S cells were able to produce tumours without oestrogen; however, WT cells did not produce any tumour.
source: C328S cells were able to produce tumours without oestrogen; however, WT cells did not produce any tumour (Figure 3O and P).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo transplantation data shown in Figure 3O and 3P.

claim: Tumour sections from C328S injected mice showed significantly higher IOD for CD56 (p<0.001) compared with IgG control.
source: Tumour sections from C328S injected mice showed significantly higher IOD for CD56 (p<0.001) (Figure 3S) and CD201 (p<0.0001) (Figure 3T) compared with IgG control.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 3S.

claim: Tumour sections from C328S injected mice showed significantly higher IOD for CD201 (p<0.0001) compared with IgG control.
source: Tumour sections from C328S injected mice showed significantly higher IOD for CD56 (p<0.001) (Figure 3S) and CD201 (p<0.0001) (Figure 3T) compared with IgG control.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 3T.

claim: Y117L substitution has been reported to assemble into ULFs and does not form long filaments.
source: Y117L substitution has been reported to assemble into ULFs (Robert et al., 2015) and does not form long filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robert et al., 2015.

claim: Transplantation of MCF-7Y117L-VIM did not induce tumour formation in nude mice, whereas MCF-7DMT-VIM did produce tumours.
source: Interestingly transplantation of MCF-7Y117L-VIM did not induce tumour formation in nude mice, whereas MCF-7DMT-VIM did produce tumours (Figure 3—figure supplement 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo transplantation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5H.

claim: Tumour progression by C328S was specific and in DMT it was dominant over Y117L.
source: These experiments suggest that tumour progression by C328S was specific and in DMT it was dominant over Y117L.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the in vivo transplantation data.

claim: Mutant vimentin was downregulated by shRNA to more than 90% as determined by RT-qPCR (p<0.01).
source: To determine whether the effects of C328S-VIM in MCF-7 can be reversed, we downregulated mutant vimentin or XIST in C328S-VIM cells by shRNA to more than 90 and 75%, respectively, as determined by RT-qPCR (p<0.01) (Figure 4A and B) and western blotting (p<0.001) (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—source data 2) compared with NTC.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: XIST was downregulated by shRNA to 75% as determined by RT-qPCR (p<0.01).
source: To determine whether the effects of C328S-VIM in MCF-7 can be reversed, we downregulated mutant vimentin or XIST in C328S-VIM cells by shRNA to more than 90 and 75%, respectively, as determined by RT-qPCR (p<0.01) (Figure 4A and B) and western blotting (p<0.001) (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—source data 2) compared with NTC.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: XIST RNA levels were reduced by 30% upon vimentin knockdown.
source: XIST RNA levels were reduced by 30% upon vimentin knockdown and VIM mRNA was downregulated by up to 20% (p<0.05) upon XIST knockdown (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: VIM mRNA was downregulated by up to 20% (p<0.05) upon XIST knockdown.
source: XIST RNA levels were reduced by 30% upon vimentin knockdown and VIM mRNA was downregulated by up to 20% (p<0.05) upon XIST knockdown (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The adhesion capacity of cells treated with VIM-shRNA was significantly increased (p<0.001) (up to 54%±1.9) but not much with XIST shRNA compared to NTC in C328S-VIM cells.
source: CyQUANT adhesion assay showed that the adhesion capacity of cells treated with VIM-shRNA was significantly increased (p<0.001) (up to 54%±1.9) but not much with XIST shRNA compared to NTC in C328S-VIM cells (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by CyQUANT adhesion assay data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: Cell proliferation, migration, and invasion were decreased upon shRNA treatment but the results were significant (p<0.05) only for the invasion assay.
source: Furthermore, cell proliferation (Figure 4I and J), migration (Figure 4K and L), and invasion (Figure 4M and N) were also decreased but the results were significant (p<0.05) only for the invasion assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 4I-N.

claim: Several morphological features including changes in cell area (p<0.01), nuclear/cell area (p<0.01), cell diameter (p<0.01), cell perimeter (p<0.01), cell major axis (p<0.05), and cell minor axis (p<0.05), were significantly reversed in MCF-7C328S-shVIM cells.
source: Morphological analysis of MCF-7C328S-shVIM cells showed that several features (not all, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1), including changes in cell area (p<0.01), nuclear/cell area (p<0.01), cell diameter (p<0.01), cell perimeter (p<0.01), cell major axis (p<0.05), and cell minor axis (p<0.05), were significantly reversed (Figure 4O).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: C328S-VIM is primarily responsible for the loss of adhesion and altered morphology of these cells.
source: These results show that C328S-VIM is primarily responsible for the loss of adhesion and altered morphology of these cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the shRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of CD56 and CD201 expression upon shRNA treatment in C328S-VIM cells showed insignificant differences, demonstrating that the expression of cancer stem cell markers was irreversible.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of CD56 and CD201 expression upon shRNA treatment in these cells showed insignificant differences (Figure 4P and Q, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), demonstrating that the expression of cancer stem cell markers was irreversible.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4P, 4Q, and supplementary figures.

claim: Earlier studies have implicated vimentin filaments in the maintenance of cell shape and increasing vimentin levels are positively related to a mesenchymal elongated phenotype and EMT.
source: Earlier studies have implicated vimentin filaments in the maintenance of cell shape and increasing vimentin levels are positively related to a mesenchymal elongated phenotype and EMT (Mendez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendez et al., 2010.

claim: The ectopic expression of the wildtype vimentin in MCF-7 can make them less elongated.
source: In contrast, we have recently shown that the ectopic expression of the wildtype vimentin in MCF-7 can make them less elongated (Usman et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Usman et al., 2022a.

claim: Cancer cells can express a wide spectrum of morphologies depending upon inducing factor and stage of EMT.
source: A possible explanation for these conflicting reports may be that cancer cells can express a wide spectrum of morphologies depending upon inducing factor and stage of EMT (Leggett et al., 2016; Sinha et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leggett et al., 2016 and Sinha et al., 2020.

claim: The C328 residue may be an active player in vimentin-linked cell phenotypic changes since downregulation of the mutant vimentin significantly reversed the morphological changes.
source: As the C328S substitution in vimentin has increased the nuclear size and made the MCF-7 cells more rounded compared to WT vimentin, it is possible that the C328 residue may be an active player in vimentin-linked cell phenotypic changes since downregulation of the mutant vimentin significantly reversed the morphological changes (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the morphological analysis and knockdown experiments.

claim: The expression of WT vimentin in MCF-7 induces cell migration without affecting proliferation or cell adhesion.
source: We have previously shown that the expression of WT vimentin in MCF-7 induces cell migration without affecting proliferation or cell adhesion (Usman et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Usman et al., 2022a.

claim: C328S-VIM enhances cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and reduces cell adhesion, which are features closely associated with EMT-mediated cancer metastasis.
source: Here we show that C328S-VIM enhances cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and reduces cell adhesion, which are features closely associated with EMT-mediated cancer metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from functional assays.

claim: Some of the changes induced by C328S-VIM could be reversed by RNAi-mediated downregulation of vimentin establishing a direct link between residue 328 of vimentin, or perhaps the surrounding region, in cancer progression.
source: Some of these changes could be reversed by RNAi-mediated downregulation of vimentin establishing a direct link between residue 328 of vimentin, or perhaps the surrounding region, in cancer progression, which is a novel finding.
evidence: This claim is supported by shRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: The increase in malignant characteristics of C328S cells implies that the original cysteine residue in vimentin acts as a tumour suppressor.
source: The increase in malignant characteristics of C328S cells implies that the original cysteine residue in vimentin acts as a tumour suppressor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in malignant characteristics upon C328S mutation.

claim: There are three major keratins, including K8 (type II), K18, and K19 (both type I), that are expressed in MCF-7.
source: There are three major keratins, including K8 (type II), K18, and K19 (both type I), that are expressed in MCF-7, and since all of them were downregulated (Figure 3), a central mechanism involved in the expression of all three keratins is likely to be affected by C328-VIM.
evidence: This is a statement about keratin expression in MCF-7 cells, drawing from established knowledge and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: A central mechanism involved in the expression of all three keratins is likely to be affected by C328-VIM.
source: There are three major keratins, including K8 (type II), K18, and K19 (both type I), that are expressed in MCF-7, and since all of them were downregulated (Figure 3), a central mechanism involved in the expression of all three keratins is likely to be affected by C328-VIM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that all three keratins were downregulated.

claim: One such mechanism is the involvement of transcription factor AP-1, which participates in the regulation of most keratin genes.
source: One such mechanism is the involvement of transcription factor AP-1, which participates in the regulation of most keratin genes (Blumenberg, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blumenberg, 2000.

claim: The transcriptomic analysis suggests that none of the AP-1 subunits are affected by C328S-VIM.
source: AP-1 is a complex of multiple different subunits (Wu et al., 2021), but our transcriptomic analysis suggests that none of these are affected by C328S-VIM (DEG lists provided in the supplementary material).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and a citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: It is conceivable that C328S-VIM could suppress AP-1 activity, thereby switching off keratin gene expression.
source: It is therefore conceivable that C328S-VIM could suppress AP-1 activity, thereby switching off keratin gene expression.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed downregulation of keratins.

claim: Multiple breast cancer stem cell markers such as POU5F1, CD56, CD49f, and CD201/PROCR were upregulated by C328-VIM, demonstrating increased stemness characteristics in MCF-7 cells.
source: Multiple breast cancer stem cell markers such as POU5F1 (Vezzoni and Parmiani, 2008), CD56 (Moghbeli et al., 2014), CD49f (Zhang et al., 2020), and CD201/PROCR (Hwang-Verslues et al., 2009) were also upregulated by C328-VIM, demonstrating increased stemness characteristics in MCF-7 cells as judged by the RNA-Seq analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and citations to prior research.

claim: Higher expression of the two stem cell markers, CD56 and CD201, was further validated by flow cytometry and also observed in vivo.
source: Higher expression of the two stem cell markers, CD56 and CD201, was further validated by flow cytometry and also observed in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Breast oncologists broadly stratify breast cancers into triple positive, borderline, and triple negative.
source: Breast oncologists broadly stratify breast cancers into triple positive, borderline, and triple negative (Orrantia-Borunda et al., 2022), which is indicative of their susceptibility to metastasise and their clinical course.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Orrantia-Borunda et al., 2022.

claim: Triple-positive breast cancers have a relatively good prognosis, followed by borderline and triple-negative lesions having by far the worst prognosis.
source: Triple-positive breast cancers have a relatively good prognosis, followed by borderline and triple-negative lesions having by far the worst prognosis (Orrantia-Borunda et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Orrantia-Borunda et al., 2022.

claim: Wildtype vimentin does not affect the expression of ESR1, PGR, and HER2 receptors in MCF-7.
source: We have previously shown that wildtype vimentin does not affect the expression of these receptors in MCF-7 (Usman et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Usman et al., 2022a.

claim: C328S-VIM makes MCF-7, a triple-positive cell line, into triple reduced, which has important clinical implications.
source: In the present study, however, C328S-VIM makes MCF-7, a triple-positive cell line (Comşa et al., 2015), into triple reduced, which has important clinical implications.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and a citation to Comşa et al., 2015.

claim: A mechanism exists whereby disruption of molecular interactions between vimentin and actin caused by C328S, directly or indirectly, regulates the expression of ESR1, PGR, and HER2 receptors, cancer progression, and metastasis.
source: It also suggests that a mechanism exists whereby disruption of molecular interactions between vimentin and actin caused by C328S, directly or indirectly, regulates the expression of these receptors, cancer progression, and metastasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of C328S-VIM.

claim: XIST is known to induce proliferation, invasion, and inhibit apoptosis in breast cancer.
source: The gene most upregulated by the C328S vimentin, as found in the RNA-Seq analysis, which is a long non-coding RNA XIST, is known to induce proliferation, invasion, and inhibit apoptosis in breast cancer (Zong et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zong et al., 2020.

claim: XIST is reported to be upregulated in multiple solid tumours.
source: It is also reported to be upregulated in multiple solid tumours (Madhi and Kim, 2019; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Madhi and Kim, 2019 and Yang et al., 2021.

claim: A recent study has unveiled XIST's gatekeeping role in human mammary epithelium homeostasis, especially the differentiation aspect in human mammary stem cells (MaSCs).
source: A recent study has unveiled its gatekeeping role in human mammary epithelium homeostasis, especially the differentiation aspect in human mammary stem cells (MaSCs) (Richart et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Richart et al., 2022.

claim: The vimentin C328S mutation is inducing EMT-like changes via XIST upregulation as downregulation of XIST in C328S cells significantly reduced proliferation and invasion.
source: It therefore appears, based on our observations, that the vimentin C328S mutation is inducing EMT-like changes via XIST upregulation as downregulation of XIST in C328S cells significantly reduced proliferation and invasion.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the shRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: The presence of C328S-VIM in MCF-7, which are oestrogen-dependent tumorigenic cells, made these cells oestrogen-independent in nude mice that further supports the in vitro data that C328S substitution had enhanced cancer stemness in MCF-7 cells.
source: A highly significant and interesting observation was that the presence of C328S-VIM in MCF-7, which are oestrogen-dependent tumorigenic cells (Soule and McGrath, 1980), made these cells oestrogen-independent in nude mice that further supports our in vitro data that C328S substitution had enhanced cancer stemness in MCF-7 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo transplantation data and a citation to Soule and McGrath, 1980.

claim: The C328 in vimentin is an important regulator of cancer cell behaviour and alterations in this region of the protein promote EMT-like changes and may induce metastasis.
source: These data suggest that the C328 in vimentin is an important regulator of cancer cell behaviour and that alterations in this region of the protein promote EMT-like changes and may induce metastasis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wildtype vimentin has been shown to increase malignant progression in lung cancer.
source: Recently, wildtype vimentin has been shown to increase malignant progression in lung cancer.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research findings.

claim: Wildtype vimentin is non-tumorigenic in breast cancer, inferring that the effect of vimentin in cancer may be tissue specific.
source: However, our data suggest that wildtype vimentin is non-tumorigenic in breast cancer, inferring that the effect of vimentin in cancer may be tissue specific, which has never been reported (Berr et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and a citation to Berr et al., 2023.

claim: Previous studies have described the importance of the C328 residue in filament assembly and organisation, stress response, aggresome formation, and lysosomal positioning only in SW13/cl.2 vimentin-deficient cells.
source: Previous studies have described the importance of the C328 residue in filament assembly and organisation, stress response, aggresome formation, and lysosomal positioning only in SW13/cl.2 vimentin-deficient cells (Pérez-Sala et al., 2015; Viedma-Poyatos et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pérez-Sala et al., 2015 and Viedma-Poyatos et al., 2020.

claim: The use of SW13/cl.2 cell model may not be appropriate to study the role of C328-VIM in EMT because these cells do not express any IFs.
source: However, the use of SW13/cl.2 cell model may not be appropriate to study the role of C328-VIM in EMT because these cells do not express any IFs.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior research models.

claim: For a cancer cell to undergo EMT, it must be an epithelial cancer cell-expressing keratin.
source: For a cancer cell to undergo EMT, it must be an epithelial cancer cell-expressing keratin.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about EMT.

claim: The use of MCF-7 in this study is most appropriate because it does not express endogenous vimentin.
source: In that respect, the use of MCF-7 in this study is most appropriate because it does not express endogenous vimentin.
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of cell model based on its characteristics.

claim: Mutations in vimentin have been reported in patients around the area of C328.
source: As mutations in vimentin have been reported in patients around the area of C328 (Usman et al., 2021), our hypothesis that this mutation induces conformational changes that activate the complex processes of EMT in breast cancer cells would have clinical implications.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Usman et al., 2021.

claim: The C328 mutation induces conformational changes that activate the complex processes of EMT in breast cancer cells.
source: As mutations in vimentin have been reported in patients around the area of C328 (Usman et al., 2021), our hypothesis that this mutation induces conformational changes that activate the complex processes of EMT in breast cancer cells would have clinical implications.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cysteine 328 in vimentin dictates mechano-transduction signals to remodel actin cytoskeleton and protect against EMT and cancer growth via modulating lncRNA XIST.
source: Altogether, our studies provide insight into how cysteine 328 in vimentin dictates mechano-transduction signals to remodel actin cytoskeleton and protect against EMT and cancer growth via modulating lncRNA XIST.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: Targeting vimentin and/or XIST via RNA interference should be a promising therapeutic strategy for breast cancer treatment.
source: Therefore, targeting vimentin and/or XIST via RNA interference should be a promising therapeutic strategy for breast cancer treatment.
evidence: This is a therapeutic recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: C328 of vimentin modifies actin organisation in response to oxidants and electrophiles.
source: It has recently been reported that C328 of vimentin modifies actin organisation in response to oxidants and electrophiles (González-Jiménez et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to González-Jiménez et al., 2023.

claim: A local perturbation at C328 (in this case by C328S substitution) can disrupt actin organisation even when cells are not exposed to oxidants and electrophiles.
source: Our data support these findings and suggest that a local perturbation at C328 (in this case by C328S substitution) can disrupt actin organisation even when cells are not exposed to oxidants and electrophiles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Vimentin is no longer a mere marker of EMT and metastasis, but appears to be an active participant in cancer progression.
source: In summary, this study highlights that vimentin is no longer a mere marker of EMT and metastasis, but appears to be an active participant in cancer progression.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: The strong correlation between the single cysteine residue at position 328 in vimentin with actin organisation, XIST induction, and hyperproliferation associated with breast oncogenesis is novel.
source: The strong correlation between the single cysteine residue at position 328 in vimentin with actin organisation, XIST induction, and hyperproliferation associated with breast oncogenesis is novel.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: C328 in vimentin remodels actin cytoskeleton and protects against EMT and cancer growth via modulating lncRNA, XIST.
source: This suggests that C328 in vimentin remodels actin cytoskeleton and protects against EMT and cancer growth via modulating lncRNA, XIST.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Targeting vimentin via RNA interference should be considered a therapeutic strategy for breast cancer treatment.
source: Taken together, we propose that targeting vimentin via RNA interference should be considered a therapeutic strategy for breast cancer treatment.
evidence: This is a therapeutic recommendation based on the experimental findings.
